chapters.title: The Maine and the blockade of Cuba
arrows: Sampson's squadron sails from Key West to blockade Havana (22 April)
Cervera's squadron crosses to Martinique, Curaçao and Santiago (29 April – 19 May)
Sampson's squadron shells San Juan, Puerto Rico (12 May)
Schley's Flying Squadron finds Cervera at Santiago (late May)
US Marines land at Guantánamo Bay (10 June)
chapters.text: On 15 February 1898 the American battleship Maine blew up in Havana harbour, killing about 260 of her crew. The cause is still debated, but "Remember the Maine!" became a rallying cry for war against Spain, whose harsh campaign against Cuban rebels had already outraged Americans. On 21–22 April American warships under William Sampson began blockading Cuba, and by 25 April the two countries were at war. Sampson shelled San Juan in Puerto Rico on 12 May while hunting for Admiral Cervera's squadron, which slipped into Santiago de Cuba on 19 May and was soon trapped there; on 10 June US Marines landed at Guantánamo Bay to win a sheltered harbour for the fleet.

chapters.title: Manila Bay and the Filipino rising
arrows: Dewey's squadron enters Manila Bay and lands at Cavite (30 April – 2 May)
Aguinaldo's revolutionaries take Cavite province (28–31 May)
The revolution spreads south to Laguna and Batangas (June)
The revolution spreads north to Bulacan and Pampanga (June)
chapters.text: Commodore George Dewey's Asiatic Squadron sailed from near Hong Kong on 27 April and entered Manila Bay on the night of 30 April. At dawn on 1 May it destroyed Admiral Montojo's squadron off Cavite without losing a man in battle, and on 2 May Dewey landed Marines at Cavite. He brought the exiled rebel leader Emilio Aguinaldo back on 19 May, and by the end of the month Filipino revolutionaries held all of Cavite province. By 9 June they controlled the provinces around Manila Bay and had laid siege to Manila, and on 12 June Aguinaldo proclaimed the independence of the Philippines at Kawit.

chapters.title: Daiquirí to San Juan Hill
arrows: Shafter's Fifth Corps lands at Daiquirí (22 June)
The army moves along the coast to Siboney (23 June)
Wheeler's cavalry attacks at Las Guásimas (24 June)
Lawton's division attacks El Caney (1 July)
Kent's and Sumner's divisions storm Kettle Hill and San Juan Hill (1 July)
chapters.text: From 22 June General William Shafter's Fifth Army Corps came ashore unopposed at Daiquirí and Siboney, east of Santiago de Cuba, as the Spanish garrisons pulled back and Cuban rebels skirmished with them. On 24 June dismounted cavalry, among them Theodore Roosevelt's Rough Riders, fought the Spanish rearguard at Las Guásimas, which then fell back towards the city. On 1 July about 15,000 American troops, helped by Cuban forces, attacked some 1,270 entrenched Spaniards: Henry Lawton's division took El Caney after a day's fighting, while cavalry stormed Kettle Hill and infantry took San Juan Hill. More than 200 Americans were killed and about 1,200 wounded, but they now held the heights above the city.

chapters.title: The capture of Guam
arrows: USS Charleston and three troopships arrive at Apra Harbor (20–21 June)
chapters.text: On its way to Manila with three troopships, the cruiser USS Charleston under Captain Henry Glass entered Apra Harbor on Guam on 20 June and fired a few shots at an abandoned fort. The island's Spanish officials had not heard that war had broken out and thought the firing was a salute. On 21 June Governor Juan Marina surrendered with his garrison of 54 soldiers, who were taken away as prisoners. The Americans raised their flag but left no troops behind when they sailed on 22 June.

chapters.title: The sea battle and the surrender of Santiago
arrows: Cervera's squadron breaks out of Santiago harbour (3 July)
The blockading fleet chases Cervera's ships along the coast (3 July)
Lawton's division extends the siege lines north of the city (2–10 July)
American troops enter Santiago (17 July)
chapters.text: With American troops on the heights above the city, Admiral Cervera was ordered to break out, and on the morning of 3 July his four cruisers and two destroyers steamed out of the harbour one by one. The blockading fleet chased them west along the coast and wrecked them all; the last, the Cristóbal Colón, ran aground after a 50-mile chase. About 343 Spaniards were killed and some 1,600 to 1,900 captured, against one American killed. Besieged by American and Cuban forces, General José Toral agreed to surrender the city and the other Spanish troops of the Santiago district, and his men marched out on 17 July.

chapters.title: Puerto Rico
arrows: Miles's convoy from Guantánamo lands at Guánica (21–25 July)
Garretson's column takes Yauco (25–26 July)
The navy takes Ponce and the army marches in (27–28 July)
Hains's brigade lands at Arroyo and takes Guayama (2–5 August)
Brooke's men push north from Guayama to the Guamaní heights (9 August)

Wilson's advance is checked at Asomante (12 August)
Schwan's brigade marches west to San Germán and Mayagüez (9–11 August)
Henry's column moves north to Adjuntas and Utuado (August)
chapters.text: General Nelson Miles avoided the fortified north coast, and on 25 July his first 1,300 men landed at Guánica in the south after a brief skirmish. Yauco fell the next day, and on 28 July Ponce, the largest city in the south, surrendered to the navy without a fight; landings at Arroyo led to the capture of Guayama on 5 August. Columns then pushed inland, taking Coamo on 9 August and Mayagüez in the west on 11 August, but Spanish and Puerto Rican troops held the mountain pass at Asomante. Fighting stopped on 13 August, when word came of the armistice signed in Washington the day before, with San Juan still in Spanish hands.

chapters.title: The Battle of Manila and the armistice
arrows: American troops move up from Cavite to the lines south of Manila (July)
Dewey's ships shell Fort San Antonio Abad (13 August)
Greene's brigade advances through Malate to Binondo (13 August)
MacArthur's brigade advances along the Pasay road (13 August)
chapters.text: By the end of July more than 10,000 American troops had landed near Manila, while some 40,000 Filipino revolutionaries held trenches around Manila. Spain's governor-general Fermín Jáudenes secretly agreed with Dewey and General Wesley Merritt to surrender the city to the Americans, not to the Filipinos, after a short show of resistance. On 13 August, unaware that Spain and the United States had signed a peace protocol in Washington the day before, American troops advanced through Malate and took Manila, though real fighting broke out and men were killed on both sides. Filipino forces were kept out of the city, a grievance that helped lead to the Philippine–American War in 1899.

battles.name: Bombardment of San Juan (naval)
battles.casualties: About 2 killed and 38 wounded on the Spanish side; 1–2 killed and 7 wounded in the American squadron

battles.name: Battle of Guantánamo Bay
battles.casualties: About 29 American killed and wounded; Spanish losses of some 200 killed and wounded and 18 captured

battles.name: Battle of Manila Bay (naval)
battles.casualties: 77 Spanish killed and 271 wounded, the whole squadron lost; 9 Americans wounded and none killed in action

battles.name: Battle of Alapan
battles.casualties: 132 Spanish killed and more than 200 captured; Filipino losses unknown

battles.name: Capture of Guam
battles.casualties: No shots returned and no one hurt; the governor and 54 Spanish soldiers taken prisoner

battles.name: Battle of Las Guásimas
battles.casualties: 17 American killed and 52 wounded; Spanish losses reported as 7 killed and 14 wounded (some accounts give more)

battles.name: Battle of El Caney
battles.casualties: Of about 500 Spanish defenders, 38 killed, 138 wounded and 160 captured; several hundred American killed and wounded

battles.name: Battle of San Juan Hill
battles.casualties: About 144 American killed, 1,024 wounded and 72 missing; 58 Spanish killed, 366 wounded and 41 captured

battles.name: Battle of Santiago de Cuba (naval)
battles.casualties: 343 Spanish killed, 151 wounded and some 1,600–1,900 captured, all six ships lost; 1 American killed and 1 wounded

battles.name: Battle of Yauco
battles.casualties: 2 Spanish killed and 5 wounded; 4 American casualties

battles.name: Battle of Silva Heights
battles.casualties: 3 Spanish killed, 6 wounded and 136 captured; 2 American killed and 15 wounded

battles.name: Battle of Asomante
battles.casualties: About a dozen Americans wounded; about 7 Spanish and Puerto Rican soldiers lost

battles.name: Battle of Manila
battles.casualties: About 49 Spanish killed; American losses given as 6 to 19 killed and about 100 wounded
